<!-- REVIEW: "final chapter" / "last inferential procedure": the roadmap still plans a chi-square
     preview and a "Choosing your test" capstone. Check this wording is what you want. -->
In this chapter we'll introduce the last inferential procedure that we will cover: regression. This extends our ability to analyze relationships among variables, much like ANOVA extends our ability to analyze differences among groups beyond what the $t$ test is capable of. And as we'll see, regression is actually a variation of the ANOVA technique itself.

## Making a prediction

Last chapter we looked at data from a study on coffee consumption and test performance. We found a negative correlation between the two variables, meaning that students who drank more coffee tended to score lower on the exam. We also found that knowing how well a student slept could help understand that relationship. The correlation and partial correlation show the strength of these relationships.

But suppose a student missed the exam and is taking a makeup. If you knew how many cups of coffee this new student had drunk that morning, could you make a guess about how they're likely to do on the exam?

<!-- quiz:
- say she drank exactly the average amount of coffee, one cup. What score would you guess she got? (The mean of the seven students' scores is 70, so that would be a reasonable guess.)
- say she drank more than average, a cup and a half. What score would you guess she got? Would guessing average test score still be the best best? (The correlation is negative, so we would guess lower than 70.)
- if you had to predict a precise score, what would it be? (We don't have enough information to make a precise prediction from the correlation alone. But what's the thought process? look at that part of the scatterplot, pick a typical score. implicitly picturing a line?) -->

If all we had to go on were the seven test scores---we had no knowledge of how much coffee the student drank---a reasonable guess would be their mean, 70. Shown as a line on the scatterplot, that kind of prediction would be a flat line going all the way across at 70. It shows that we would be making the same guess for everyone, regardless of their coffee consumption.

But suppose we let the line tilt, so we can give a different answer depending on how much coffee someone drank. That makes use of the relationship between the two variables. We found a negative correlation, $r = -.50$, so the line should slope downward; as coffee consumption increases, our predicted test score should decrease. But by how much? How would we know which line is best?

## Straight lines

A brief reminder about straight lines. (I'm guessing you're familiar with this from high school math.) A line on a graph is defined by two things: its slope, $b$, and its intercept, $a$.[^symbols] The slope tells us how steep the line is. This is often described as the "rise over run," or how much the line goes up or down for each unit it moves to the right. The intercept tells us where it crosses the $Y$ axis---what the value of $Y$ is when $X$ equals zero.

That gives the equation for a straight line:

$$ Y = bX + a $$ {#eq-straight-line}

[^symbols]: These symbols aren't universal. When I learned this stuff in school, we used $m$ for the slope and $c$ for the intercept. There are both regional and disciplinary differences in the notation. In statistics, $b$ and $a$ are the most common symbols for slope and intercept.

A straight line you might already be familiar with is the relationship between temperatures on the Celsius scale and on the Fahrenheit scale.

::: {#fig-temperature-slope-intercept}

{{< interactive-figure celsiusFahrenheitParts makeScatterplot options='{"points":[[0,32],[10,50],[20,68],[30,86],[40,104],[50,122]],"xLabel":"Celsius (°C)","yLabel":"Fahrenheit (°F)","xDomain":[0,50],"yDomain":[0,130],"line":"fit","maxWidth":"30rem","controls":false,"showPoints":false,"guide":0,"riseRun":{"from":10,"to":20}}' fallback="The Celsius–Fahrenheit line. A guide marks 32 °F where the line meets the Y axis. From 10 to 20 °C, a run of 10 degrees Celsius, the line rises 18 °F." >}}

[Placeholder caption: the intercept, 32 °F at 0 °C, and the slope as rise over run: 18 °F over 10 °C, so 1.8 °F per degree Celsius.]

:::

The relationship between the scales can be expressed as $Y = 1.8X + 32$. Zero degrees Celsius corresponds to 32 Fahrenheit; that's the intercept. $1.8$ is the slope: how much $Y$ changes per unit change in $X$. For an increase of one degree Celsius, Fahrenheit increases by 1.8 degrees. We can covert any temperature from one scale to the other using this equation. Like, 100 degrees Celsius is 212 degrees Fahrenheit: $Y = 1.8(100) + 32 = 212$.

Obviously the relationship between these two variables is a perfect correlation. If we took some values of Celsius and their corresponding Fahrenheit values, we could calculate the correlation and it would come out to 1. But the slope is 1.8, not 1. They're related, but they answer different questions. The slope tells us how steep that line is, in the units we measured. Together with the intercept, this is what allows us to make predictions.

### The line of best fit

So how does this help us when we have a bunch of data that isn't perfectly correlated? Simple: we draw a line though the points to summarize their relationship. It gives a typical value on the $Y$ variable for any given value of $X$. Then we use the line to make predictions, just like we convert Celsius to Fahrenheit. Use the slider to read off the prediction for our student who drank a cup and a half.

{{< interactive-figure bestFitLineScatter makeScatterplot options='{"points":[[0,90],[0.5,60],[0.5,85],[1,65],[1.5,50],[1.5,65],[2,75]],"xLabel":"Coffee (cups)","yLabel":"Test score","xDomain":[0,2.5],"yDomain":[40,100],"line":"fit","controls":false,"maxWidth":"30rem","guide":0.5,"showSliders":["guide"],"sliders":[{"key":"guide","range":[0,2.5,0.5],"tex":"{x}\\\\text{ cups: } {y}\\\\text{ points}","readoutWidth":"9rem"}]}' fallback="The coffee and test score scatterplot with the line of best fit drawn through the points, falling from an intercept of 80 with a slope of −10. Guides read half a cup up to the line and across to 75 points, and a slider moves the reading from 0 to 2.5 cups: a cup and a half reads across to 65." >}}

You should get a predicted score of 65.

But I dodged an important issue. There are an infinite number of straight lines that we *could* draw through a scatterplot. You can easily imagine a line that's a bit lower than this one, or a bit higher, or one that's at a steeper angle, or one that's shallower. None of them will go through every data point perfectly. Every possible line will have some misses. How do we know which line is best? We find the one that minimizes the collective misses---the one that is least wrong. This is called the **line of best fit**.

To be more precise about the "misses," when a point isn't exactly on the line, it's either at some distance above or below the line of best fit. That distance gets a special name in the context of regression: a **residual**. It's the difference between the observed value, $Y$, and the predicted value, denoted $\hat{Y}$. So a residual is:

$$ Y - \hat{Y} $$

Don't let the fancy new name and symbol fool you, though. This is a familiar concept. It's a deviation, just like $X - M$. The difference is that the predicted value comes from the line of best fit rather than from the mean. The line of best like summarizes the central tendency of the relationship between two variables, just like the mean summarizes the central tendency of a single variable. But when the two variables are related, it's a moving average, giving different predictions for different values of $X$.

For example, the student who drank a cup and a half of coffee scored 50 points, but our prediction was 65. The difference is $50 - 65 = -15$. 

We call that a **prediction error**, as in, if you were predicting what the point would have been based only on the line, you would've been a bit off.

::: {#quiz-regression-prediction-error}
{{< include quizzes/18-regression-prediction-error.qmd >}}
:::

So for any line, we can compute the residuals. Something else they have in common with our old friends, deviations, is that we can square the residuals and then sum them up to get a useful quantity, the **sum of squared residuals**, $SS_{\text{residual}}$.

$$ SS_{\text{residual}} = \Sigma(Y - \hat{Y})^2 $$

So you can see how this is fundamentally the same equation we learned all those chapters ago for the sum of squared deviations. In Chapter 4 the mean gave us the smallest possible sum of squared deviations for a single guess. Here we get to choose both the height and the slope of the line. The one that minimizes the sum of squared residuals is the line of best fit. This is called **least squares**.

The line of best fit is the line that minimizes this quanity, representing the *collective* prediction error. Any other straight line through this scatterplot would've produced a larger total for $SS_{\text{residual}}$.

That's all well and good, but how do we actually find the line of best fit? Thankfully we don't have to go through every possible line to find the one that gives the smallest answer.^[Since there are infinity of them, it'd take forever.] We can find the slope and intercept of the line of best fit directly from the data.

### The slope ($b$)

In Chapter 17 we found the correlation by dividing the sum of products, $SP$, by $\sqrt{SS_X SS_Y}$. Dividing by the variability of both variables cancels out the units. For the slope we want to keep them: test points per cup of coffee. So we divide $SP$ by $SS_X$ alone. This will give us the "rise over run"; for a unit change in $X$ (given its individual variability), how much does Y change (given its association with $X$, captured by $SP$)?

We calculated both $SP$ and $SS_X$ in the previous chapter, so we already have what we need. We got $-30$ for the sum of products and 3 for the sum of squares for coffee. So here we get $-30$ over 3 for an answer of $-10$.

$$ b = \frac{SP}{SS_X} = \frac{-30}{3} = -10 $$

In other words, as you move one unit along the $X$ axis, you move down ten units on the $Y$ axis. Going from one to two on the $X$ axis, for example, if you follow the regression line along, the predicted $Y$ value moves from 70 to 60. The correlation of $-.50$ told us the line would slope down. By keeping the units, the slope tells us how far down it goes for each cup of coffee.

         In z-score units both SDs are 1, so the slope IS r. That's the cleanest single statement of

### The intercept ($a$)

Having figured out the slope, we can use it to find $a$, the intercept. Remember, this is just the value of $Y$ when $X = 0$. To figure this out, we can use that slope together with another point we know the line will pass through: the point where the means of $X$ and $Y$ intersect.

$$ a = M_Y - b M_X $$

The line captures the central tendency of the relationship, so it has to pass through that point where both scores are entirely typical. So we know that by the time the line has run from $X = 0$ to $X = M_X$, its slope will have produced a change in $Y$ of $b M_X$ to bring it to $M_Y$. Subtracting that change from $M_Y$ lets us figure out where must it have started on the $Y$ axis to get there.

<!-- Alt wording: That's what $a = M_Y - b M_X$ is working out. Think about going from zero on the $X$ axis to the mean of $X$. Each unit you move along changes the height of the line by $b$, so by the time you reach $M_X$, the height has changed by $b M_X$ altogether. To get back to where you started, take that change away from $M_Y$. -->

For our data:

$$ a = 70 - (-10) \times 1 = 80 $$

For a student who drank no coffee, we predict a score of 80.

::: {#quiz-regression-intercept}
{{< include quizzes/18-regression-intercept.qmd >}}
:::

Now we can answer our original question without reading off the graph. A cup and a half gives $\hat{Y} = -10(1.5) + 80 = 65$. The direction of the prediction matters here. If we wanted to guess how much coffee someone drank from their test score, we'd fit a line that made the misses in *cups* as small as possible. Here we're measuring the misses in test points.

<!-- REVIEW: This direction point is one of the main ways regression goes beyond r (r is symmetric; Ch 17
     even says so about the correlation matrix). Consider moving it up: to the opening, or to just after the
     Celsius–Fahrenheit section, where a sentence (cut for pace) noted that converting F → C gives a slope of 1/1.8. With r = 1 both
     directions give the same line. With r = -.50 they don't: predicting cups from score would give a line
     with slope r × s_X/s_Y = -.025 cups per point. Drawn on these axes that's -40 points per cup, much
     steeper than -10, because each line regresses toward its own mean. -->

You can see the least-squares fit in action below. We'll start with the same naive guess for everyone---that they will all just get the average test score, regardless of their coffee consumption---and see how much better we can do by letting the line tilt.

::::: {#act-least-squares .callout-tip .interactive}

What if we ignored $X$ and just guessed the mean of $Y$ every time? That's a flat line at 70. Measure each score's distance from the line, square it, and collect the squares just as we did in ANOVA. The whole square is $SS_Y = 1200$, the total variability in test score.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Best-fit line" data-action='{"collect-ss":"reference","line":"fit","show-residuals":false,"show-squares":false,"show-ss":false,"show-means":false,"controls-open":false,"emphasize":"none"}'}
The line of best fit traces the best path through the points: $\hat{Y} = -10X + 80$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Residuals" data-action='{"draw":"lines","collect-ss":"reference","line":"fit","show-residuals":true,"show-squares":false,"show-ss":false,"show-means":false,"controls-open":false,"emphasize":["residuals","points"]}'}
The vertical distance shows how far off our prediction was. For a point on the line the prediction is exactly right and the residual is zero. For every point we calculate the residual the same way, $Y - \hat{Y}$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Squares" data-action='{"draw":"squares","collect-ss":"reference","line":"fit","show-residuals":true,"show-squares":true,"show-ss":false,"show-means":false,"controls-open":false,"emphasize":"none"}'}
Square each residual---literally. The student whose score we missed by 15 points contributes a square with an area of 225.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Sum of squares" data-action='{"collect-ss":"residual","line":"fit","show-residuals":true,"show-squares":true,"show-ss":false,"show-means":false,"controls-open":false,"emphasize":"none"}'}
Collect these squares in the same outline. The student who scored exactly what we predicted contributes zero. Add up the areas for all seven students and we get $SS_{residual} = 900$. That fills three quarters of the square.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="What did the line explain?" data-action='{"collect-ss":"regression","draw":"both","line":"fit","show-residuals":true,"show-squares":true,"show-ss":false,"show-means":true,"emphasize":"none","controls-open":false}'}
This time, start at each student's prediction on the fitted line. How far is it from our old guess of 70? For half a cup we predict 75, so that's a square of 25 for each of the two students who drank half a cup. Collect all seven and we get $SS_{regression} = 300$. It fills the gap exactly. That's how much squared error we saved by using coffee to predict test score.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Least error" data-action='{"collect-ss":"compare","line":"fit","show-residuals":true,"show-squares":true,"show-ss":true,"show-means":false,"emphasize":"none","show-sliders":["slope","intercept"]}'}
Back to the residuals. Our best-fit line leaves us with 900. No other line does better---that's what makes it the least-squares fit. Don't take my word for it: use the sliders below the plot to try any slope and intercept you like. Remember the line we imagined moving down five points? Keep the slope at $-10$ and change the intercept from 80 to 75. The squared misses for all seven students now add up to 1075.
:::

## Partitioning variability

Think back to ANOVA. We started with each score's deviation from the grand mean. Knowing which group someone belonged to let us guess their group mean instead. How far the group means were from the grand mean gave us the between-groups variability. How far the scores still fell from their respective group means gave us the within-groups variability.

Notice how we've mostly been framing everything around the $Y$ variable. We're predicting $Y$, and the residuals tell us how far off we were on $Y$. So it's the variability in test scores we're partitioning here. Start at the mean test score, 70. Take the student who drank two cups and scored 75. The line takes our prediction from 70 down to 60. The student's actual score is 15 points above that prediction. Those two steps, $-10$ and $+15$, add up to the original deviation of $+5$. The first step is how far the *prediction* is from the mean. The second is the residual.

{{< interactive-figure regressionPartitionDiagram makeVariancePartitionDiagram options='{"preset":"regression","maxWidth":"38rem"}' fallback="Diagram partitioning the total variability in Y into predictable variability (sum of squares regression) and unpredictable variability (sum of squares residual), whose mean squares form the F ratio for the analysis of regression." >}}

Across the whole sample, those two sets of deviations give us the same kind of partition we used for ANOVA. The **regression sum of squares** is $SS_{regression} = \Sigma(\hat{Y} - M_Y)^2$. For the student who drank two cups, that's $(60 - 70)^2 = 100$ toward the regression sum of squares and $(75 - 60)^2 = 225$ toward the residual sum of squares. It's the *sums* that partition the total. The squares for any one student needn't add up that way.

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_Y &= SS_{regression} + SS_{residual} \\
1200 &= 300 + 900
\end{aligned}
$$

We've just seen how to calculate $SS_{residual}$. And we calculated the sum of squared deviations for $Y$ in the previous chapter. The sum of squares regression is just whatever is left over from $SS_Y - SS_{residual}$. Here that's $1200 - 900 = 300$. That's how much we reduced the squared error by letting the line tilt. What proportion of the total did that account for?

$$ r^2 = \frac{SS_{regression}}{SS_Y} = \frac{300}{1200} = .25 $$

There's the $.25$ we got by squaring $r = -.50$ in Chapter 17. In regression this proportion is called the **coefficient of determination**. It plays the same part as $\eta^2$ in ANOVA. Here, knowing coffee consumption accounts for a quarter of the variability in these seven test scores. The other three quarters, $SS_{residual}/SS_Y = 900/1200 = .75$, is the $1 - r^2$ that went into the standard error of the correlation in Chapter 17. Back then we described it as the variability unaccounted for by the relationship. Now you can see exactly what that is: the squared misses around the line.

For the degrees of freedom, $df_Y$ is the number of scores minus one, or six. One degree of freedom goes to regression for the one predictor. (The flat line at the mean already had its height; all the regression line adds is the slope.) That leaves five for the residual. Once we have those sums of squares and degrees of freedom, we do what we usually do with sums of squares and degrees of freedom. We divide them to find a kind of variance, or mean square. And those become the numerator and denominator of a new $F$ ratio for the regression.

$$ MS_{regression} = \frac{SS_{regression}}{df_{regression}} $$

$$ MS_{residual} = \frac{SS_{residual}}{df_{residual}} $$

$$ F = \frac{MS_{regression}}{MS_{residual}} $$

$MS_{residual}$ is the variance of the scores around the line, the same quantity we found on the way to the standard error of the estimate. $MS_{regression}$ is how much the line improved on the mean, per slope we estimated.

::: {#quiz-regression-flat-line}
{{< include quizzes/18-regression-flat-line.qmd >}}
:::

Suppose the slope in the population were zero. Then, just like the two estimates in Chapter 14, both mean squares would be estimating the same error variance, and we'd expect $F$ to come out around 1. A real relationship adds to $MS_{regression}$ without adding to $MS_{residual}$, so it tends to make $F$ larger. This is what we'll use for the hypothesis test.

## The standard error of the estimate

So now we have the equation to calculate our $\hat{Y}$ values. We can calculate the prediction error, the deviation of each point from the best fit line. And with that, we can square those residual deviations and sum the squares to find the sum of squared residuals, $SS_{residual}$. In Chapter 17 we subtracted 70 from every score to get its deviation from the mean. To fill in @tbl-residuals, the only thing we change is the number we subtract. For someone who drank half a cup, that's 75. For someone who drank two cups, it's 60.

| Coffee ($X$) | Test score ($Y$) | $\hat{Y}$ | $Y - \hat{Y}$ | $(Y - \hat{Y})^2$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 90 | 80 | $10$ | 100 |
| 0.5 | 60 | 75 | $-15$ | 225 |
| 0.5 | 85 | 75 | $10$ | 100 |
| 1 | 65 | 70 | $-5$ | 25 |
| 1.5 | 50 | 65 | $-15$ | 225 |
| 1.5 | 65 | 65 | $0$ | 0 |
| 2 | 75 | 60 | $15$ | 225 |

: Predicted values and residuals for the coffee data. {#tbl-residuals}

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{residual} &= \Sigma(Y - \hat{Y})^2 \\
&= 100 + 225 + 100 + 25 + 225 + 0 + 225 \\
&= 900
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {#quiz-regression-ss-df}
{{< include quizzes/18-regression-ss-df.qmd >}}
:::

In the context of regression, we talk about the **standard error of the estimate**. The $\hat{Y}$ values that make up the line of best fit give our best guess at $Y$ for any value of $X$. How much did the actual scores tend to vary around those predictions? If you think about it, that's a familiar question. We calculate the mean of a set of scores, and standard deviation quantifies how much points tended to vary around that mean. Here we want the standard deviation of points around the line of best fit.

Remember that standard deviation $s$ was found by taking the square root of the sum of squared deviations over degrees of freedom. The standard error of the estimate works the same way. Here it's the sum of squared residuals that we divide by the degrees of freedom. We used the data to estimate two things, the slope and the intercept, leaving $n - 2$ degrees of freedom.

$$ s_{\text{estimate}} = \sqrt{\frac{SS_{residual}}{n-2}} = \sqrt{\frac{900}{5}} = 13.42 $$

So our predictions for these students were typically off by about 13 test points.

Notice what we had just before taking the square root: $900/5 = 180$. That's a variance, the average squared miss around the line (in squared test points). Keep that number in mind, because it's going to turn up again.

## A regression test, step by step

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

The null here is that the slope of the regression line in the population is zero. Or put another way, it would mean that knowing someone's score on the $X$ variable would be no help in making a straight-line prediction of their score on the $Y$ variable. Our best guess would be the mean of $Y$, regardless of their score on $X$. (That's exactly the flat line we pitted against the best-fit line in the activity earlier---the one whose squared error came out to $SS_Y$.)

The alternative hypothesis is that the slope is not equal to zero. And notice that the slope we calculated based on our sample is labeled $b$. The population parameter we're interested in here is labeled with the Greek symbol $\beta$. For one predictor, asking whether $\beta$ is zero is the same question we asked about the population correlation in Chapter 17.

<!-- REVIEW: NOTATION CLASH. Published papers (APA style, including Dunn et al.) use β for STANDARDIZED
     coefficients. If multiple regression introduces standardized slopes, readers will meet β meaning two
     things. Options: keep β for the population slope and footnote the APA usage; or write H0 in words /
     with another symbol and keep β for standardized slopes, as Gravetter & Wallnau do. -->


$$ H_0: \beta = 0 $$

$$ H_1: \beta \ne 0 $$

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

Step two is to find the critical value for the test statistic. And since we're using an $F$ ratio, we use the $F$ table. The degrees of freedom for the numerator, $df_{regression}$, is one here. And for the denominator, $df_{residual}$ is $7 - 2$, which is five. With $\alpha = .05$, the critical value is 6.61. We reject the null if $F > 6.61$.

::: {#tbl-regression-critical}
{{< interactive-figure regressionCriticalTable makeFTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the coffee test","alpha":0.05,"df1":{"from":1,"to":4},"df2":{"from":3,"to":7},"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","interactive":false,"selected":{"df1":1,"df2":5,"alpha":0.05}}' fallback="F table excerpt for numerator df 1 through 4 and denominator df 3 through 7, highlighting the .05 critical value of 6.61 at F(1, 5)." >}}

An excerpt of the $F$ table for $\alpha = .05$, with the critical value for $F(1, 5)$ highlighted.
:::

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

Step three is to calculate the $F$ ratio for the data. Some of the required values we already calculated earlier in this chapter or in the previous chapter. See if you can get all the required sums of squares and degrees of freedom to calculate the numerator and denominator of the test statistic and find the $F$ ratio.

::: {#quiz-regression-calculate-f}
{{< include quizzes/18-regression-calculate-f.qmd >}}
:::

Here's the full working, so you can check your answers:

::: {#tbl-regression-summary .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Regression | 300 | 1 | 300 | 1.67 |
| Residual | 900 | 5 | 180 | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | 1200 | 6 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

Summary table for the analysis of regression on the coffee data.
:::

There's that 180 again. The denominator of our $F$ ratio is the variance of the scores around the line, and its square root, $\sqrt{180} = 13.42$, is the standard error of the estimate.

### Step 4: Make a decision

Our $F$ of 1.67 falls short of the critical value of 6.61 for $F(1, 5)$ at $\alpha = .05$. Here, as with the correlation for this data in the previous chapter, we fail to reject the null. In fact, we get the same $p = .25$ as in Chapter 17. Remember how Chapter 14's two-group $F$ was just the square of the independent-samples $t$? With one predictor, the regression $F$ is the square of the $t$ for the correlation. Here $(-1.291)^2 \approx 1.67$.

::: {#fig-regression-decision}
{{< interactive-figure regressionTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"f","df1":1,"df2":5,"title":"Null distribution: F(1, 5)","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[0,10],"yDomain":[0,1.6],"points":160,"xTicks":6,"labels":{"x":"F ratio"},"shade":{"tail":"right","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":6.607891,"label":"6.61","height":0.45,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":1.666667,"label":"F = 1.67","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null F distribution with 1 and 5 degrees of freedom. The rejection region lies beyond 6.61; the observed F of 1.67 falls short of it." >}}

The observed $F = 1.67$ falls short of the critical value of the null $F$ distribution with 1 and 5 degrees of freedom.
:::

## Reporting and interpreting the results

When we report the results, we can mention the general trend in the data as quantified in $b$, the slope of the regression line. And then we mention the $F$ ratio for the analysis of regression with its degrees of freedom and its $p$-value. We can also say how much of the variability the line accounted for.

> Each additional cup of coffee was associated with a predicted test score 10 points lower ($b = -10$). Coffee consumption accounted for 25% of the variability in scores, $F(1, 5) = 1.67$, $p = .25$.

How precisely have we estimated that ten-point drop? Just as we did for a difference between means, we can put a confidence interval around the slope. Here the 95% interval runs from about 30 points lower to 10 points higher per cup.^[The standard error of the slope is $s_b = \sqrt{MS_{residual}/SS_X} = \sqrt{180/3} = 7.75$ points per cup. Using the critical $t$ from Chapter 17 gives $-10 \pm 2.571(7.75)$. Compare it with the standard error of the mean, which we could write as $\sqrt{s^2/n}$. In both cases it's a variance divided by how much information we have. For a mean, that's the number of scores. For a slope, it's how spread out the $X$ values are: the wider the range of coffee we observed, the more precisely we can pin down the slope.] With seven students, even the direction of the population slope is uncertain.

<!-- REVIEW: extrapolation sets up restricted range (held off in Ch 17) and predicting beyond the data,
     both saved for the possible "real-world messiness" chapter. A one-line forward allusion here would do. -->

There's also a limit to where it makes sense to use the equation. Put eight cups into it and the predicted score is zero. Our students drank between zero and two cups. We've seen nothing to tell us what the relationship looks like out at eight. And even in the range we observed, telling someone to skip a cup of coffee is a different proposition from predicting how they'll score. What if the students who drank more coffee had also slept less?

### Regression assumptions

<!-- REVIEW: A statistical difference from Ch 17 worth one sentence. Regression assumes normally distributed
     ERRORS around the line at each X, not bivariate normality; X itself can have any distribution (even
     fixed by the researcher). The closing "What if the predictor is a group?" section depends on this, since
     a 0/1 predictor can't be normal. A residual plot (the residuals from the least-squares activity, laid
     out against X) is the natural check, and readers have already seen the residuals drawn. -->

What would we want to check in this scatterplot? Does a straight line follow the middle of the cloud? Do the vertical misses look about as spread out at one end as at the other? For the test and interval we've used, we assume independent observations and roughly normally distributed errors with similar spread at each value of $X$. That's much like checking the spread around the group means in ANOVA. Seven points give us very little to go on here.

In Chapter 17 we asked whether coffee and test scores were still related once we took sleep into account. Let's take the same seven students and turn that into a prediction question. If we knew how much sleep someone got as well as how much coffee they drank, could we make a better guess at their score?

| Participant | Coffee ($X$) | Sleep ($Z$) | Test score ($Y$) |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A | 0 | 9 | 90 |
| B | 0.5 | 8 | 60 |
| C | 0.5 | 8 | 85 |
| D | 1 | 5 | 65 |
| E | 1.5 | 6 | 50 |
| F | 1.5 | 6 | 65 |
| G | 2 | 7 | 75 |

: The seven students' coffee, sleep, and test scores, from Chapter 17. {#tbl-coffee-sleep-scores-again}

With **multiple regression**, each predictor gets its own slope. We multiply cups of coffee by one slope and hours of sleep by the other, then add the intercept. We still choose the values that make the sum of squared misses as small as possible.

$$ \hat{Y} = b_1 X + b_2 Z + a $$ {#eq-multiple-regression}

<!-- REVIEW (point 6, parked): this is the one place results simply appear. A possible lead-in:
     a quiz asking readers to predict whether coffee's slope, with sleep in the equation, will be steeper
     than −10, about the same, or flatter; then reveal −2; then the residual-on-residual tutorial
     (comment below) shows why. The "what sleep adds" quiz further down already works this way. -->

<!-- DRAFT -->
So what are the two slopes? You might think we could just reuse what we already have. Coffee's slope on its own was $-10$. Fit sleep on its own and we'd get a slope of 6.67 points per hour. So why not put both of those into one equation? If we do that, our predictions miss by a total of 900, no better than coffee alone. Sleep alone did better than that, at 666.67.

The problem is that coffee and sleep go together. The students who drank more coffee tended to sleep less. So coffee's slope of $-10$ was already carrying a lot of sleep's effect. Adding sleep's own slope on top counts that part twice. What we want for coffee is its slope once sleep has been taken out of the picture. And for that we can use the technique we used for partial correlations in Chapter 17: measuring deviations from a prediction.

<!-- DRAFT -->
### Calculating the slopes and intercept

Remember how we got the slope with one predictor. We divided the sum of products by the sum of squares for coffee, and both were built from each student's deviation from the mean coffee, $X - M_X$. To take sleep into account, we do exactly the same thing, but we measure each student's coffee from a different reference point: the amount of coffee we'd predict from their sleep, $\hat{X}$. So instead of deviations, $X - M_X$, we work with residuals, $X - \hat{X}$. 

To work out the $\hat{X}$ predictions, we regress coffee on sleep, in exactly the same way we did in the first part of the chapter with coffee and test scores, finding a slope and intercept for that relationship which we use to predict $\hat{X}$, the amount of coffee we'd expect each person to have drank for someone who slept as much as they did. Then we see how much more or less they drank than our prediction: $X - \hat{X}$. These are like the residuals we've been squaring all chapter, only for the coffee-predicting-sleep relationship instead of coffee-predicting-test-scores.

From there it's all familiar. Square the residuals and add them up, and we have a sum of squares. Multiply each one by the student's deviation from the mean score, $Y - M_Y$, and add those up, and we have a sum of products. Divide one by the other and we have the slope. If that sounds familiar, it's because it's how we got the partial correlation in Chapter 17, except that this time we only need to take sleep out of coffee.^[If you take sleep out of the test scores as well, and use their residuals instead of $Y - M_Y$, you get exactly the same slope. And the correlation between the two sets of residuals is $-.10$, the partial correlation for these seven students.]

<!-- DRAFT -->

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Coffee and sleep" data-action='{"stage":"data","animate":false}'}
Here's each student's sleep ($Z$) and coffee ($X$) again. We want to take sleep out of their coffee.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Predicted from sleep" data-action='{"stage":"predicted"}'}
First, predict each student's coffee from their sleep. That's just a regression with one predictor. Its slope is the sum of products for coffee and sleep over the sum of squares for sleep, $-4/12 = -0.33$. Each extra hour of sleep goes with a third of a cup less coffee. And like any regression line, it goes through the means: one cup at seven hours.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Residuals" data-action='{"stage":"residuals"}'}
Then subtract: each student's actual coffee minus what their sleep predicts. These are the residuals, the part of each student's coffee that sleep can't account for. Where we'd have had $X - M_X$, we now have $X - \hat{X}$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Sum of squares" data-action='{"stage":"squared"}'}
Now square the residuals and add them up, just as we squared $X - M_X$ to get the sum of squares for coffee. That was 3. For the residuals it's only 1.67, because most of the variability in coffee was predictable from sleep.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Sum of products" data-action='{"stage":"products"}'}
Multiply each residual by that student's deviation from the mean score of 70, just as we multiplied $X - M_X$ by $Y - M_Y$ to get the sum of products. That was $-30$. With the residuals it's only $-3.33$. Most of coffee's relationship with test score was running through sleep.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="The other way round" data-action='{"stage":"products","alt":true}'}
For the slope for sleep, swap the two predictors' roles. Now we predict each student's sleep from their coffee, take the residuals, and square them and multiply them by the same deviations in test score. Sleep's sum of squares on its own was 12, and taking coffee out halves it to 6.67. Its sum of products was 80, and that halves too, to 40. So sleep's slope barely changes.
:::

::::

:::::

The slope is the sum of products over the sum of squares, exactly as it was with one predictor, just using the residuals.^[The numbers in the table are rounded to two decimal places, but each was calculated from the unrounded values before it. If you work with the rounded values you'll get slightly different answers, like $-1.99$ for this slope. Unrounded, the sum of squares is exactly $5/3$ and the sum of products exactly $-10/3$, which gives exactly $-2$.]

$$ b_1 = \frac{-3.33}{1.67} = -2 $$

To get $b_2$, the slope for sleep, we do the same thing the other way round, with the part of sleep that coffee doesn't predict, as in the last step of @act-coffee-residuals. That gives a sum of squares of 6.67 and a sum of products of 40, so $b_2 = 40 / 6.67 = 6$.^[There's also a shortcut for these sums, without the column of residuals: take out the part that runs through the other predictor. For coffee, $SS_X - SP_{XZ}^2/SS_Z$ $= 3 - (-4)^2/12$ $= 1.67$ and $SP_{XY} - SP_{XZ}\,SP_{ZY}/SS_Z$ $= -30 - (-4)(80)/12$ $= -3.33$. For sleep, $SS_Z - SP_{XZ}^2/SS_X$ $= 12 - (-4)^2/3$ $= 6.67$ and $SP_{ZY} - SP_{XZ}\,SP_{XY}/SS_X$ $= 80 - (-4)(-30)/3$ $= 40$.]

Like the line with one predictor, the equation passes through the means: one cup, seven hours, and 70 points. So to find the intercept, we start from the mean score and take away what the two slopes add at the mean coffee and mean sleep: $a = 70 - (-2)(1) - 6(7) = 30$.

<!-- DRAFT: your sentence was "Fitting that equation to our seven students gives us a slope of $-2$ for coffee and
     $6$ for sleep. The intercept is 30." It now follows the working, so it's a summary; the footnote is unchanged. -->
So the slope for coffee is $-2$, the slope for sleep is 6, and the intercept is 30.

$$ \hat{Y} = -2X + 6Z + 30 $$

Try the equation for someone who slept six hours and drank a cup and a half. We get $-2(1.5) + 6(6) + 30 = 63$. Now keep sleep at six hours and change coffee from one and a half cups to half a cup. The predicted score goes up by just two points. With coffee alone that same change raised the prediction by ten points. That's what the coffee slope means *with sleep in the equation*. Likewise, holding coffee constant, each extra hour of sleep raises the predicted score by six points.

<!-- DRAFT -->
Notice what happens if we fix sleep at a particular value. For someone who slept nine hours, the equation becomes $-2X + 6(9) + 30$, or $-2X + 84$. That's just an ordinary straight line, with a slope of $-2$ and an intercept of 84. Every amount of sleep gives a line like that, all with the same slope, each 6 points above the one for an hour less. You'll see those lines in the activity below.

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Coffee alone" data-action='{"collect-ss":"residual","line":"fit","color-z":false,"show-residuals":true,"show-squares":true,"show-means":false,"emphasize":"none","animate":false}'}
Here's where we left off: coffee on its own, the line of best fit, and its squared misses filling three quarters of the square.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Sleep" data-action='{"collect-ss":"reference","line":"fit","color-z":true,"show-residuals":false,"show-squares":false,"show-means":false,"emphasize":"none"}'}
Now color each student by how long they slept, darker for more sleep. The darker dots tend to sit toward the left. The students who slept more drank less coffee.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Coffee at average sleep" data-action='{"collect-ss":"reference","line":"adjusted","adjust-x":true,"rise-run":{"from":0,"to":1},"color-z":true,"show-residuals":false,"show-squares":false,"show-means":false,"emphasize":"none"}'}
Now add the average of one cup back on to each student's residual from @act-coffee-residuals. That's their coffee as it would be if they'd slept an average seven hours. Students who slept more move right, and students who slept less move left. Watch the line follow them. Through the adjusted dots it's much flatter, with the slope for coffee once sleep is taken into account, $b_1$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="A line for each amount of sleep" data-action='{"collect-ss":"reference","line":"multiple","rise-run":{"from":0,"to":1},"show-spacing":true,"color-z":true,"show-residuals":false,"show-squares":false,"show-means":false,"emphasize":"none"}'}
Now put the dots back where they really are. The flatter line runs through the means, so it's our prediction for someone with an average seven hours of sleep. Each extra hour lifts the prediction by the slope for sleep, $b_2$, and each hour less lowers it by the same amount. So every amount of sleep gets its own line, all with the same slope.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="One student" data-action='{"draw":"both","focus":[0],"collect-ss":"reference","line":"multiple","color-z":true,"show-residuals":true,"show-squares":true,"show-means":false,"emphasize":"none"}'}
Now we measure the misses just as before. This student drank no coffee and slept nine hours, so we read their prediction off the nine-hour line. They scored a little higher than that. And we square the miss.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Another student" data-action='{"draw":"both","focus":[0,3],"collect-ss":"reference","line":"multiple","color-z":true,"show-residuals":true,"show-squares":true,"show-means":false,"emphasize":"none"}'}
This student slept just five hours. Their dot happens to sit between the six- and seven-hour lines, but that doesn't matter. Their prediction comes from the five-hour line, because that's how long they slept.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Everyone" data-action='{"draw":"both","collect-ss":"reference","line":"multiple","color-z":true,"show-residuals":true,"show-squares":true,"show-means":false,"emphasize":"none"}'}
And the same for everyone else, each measured from the line for their own amount of sleep.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Sum of squares" data-action='{"collect-ss":"residual","line":"multiple","color-z":true,"show-residuals":true,"show-squares":true,"show-means":false,"emphasize":"none"}'}
Collect the squares. The dashed outlines show how each predictor did on its own. Adding sleep to coffee brings the total down a lot. Adding coffee to sleep barely moves it at all.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="What did both explain?" data-action='{"collect-ss":"regression","draw":"both","line":"multiple","color-z":true,"show-residuals":true,"show-squares":true,"show-means":true,"emphasize":"none"}'}
As before, the rest of the square is what our predictions saved us compared with just guessing the mean. Measure from each student's prediction to the mean and collect those squares. They fill the gap exactly.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Who explained what?" data-action='{"collect-ss":"partition","line":"multiple","color-z":true,"show-residuals":true,"show-squares":true,"show-means":true,"emphasize":"none"}'}
Just like we split between-groups variability into factors in Chapter 16, we can split this up. Some of it only sleep accounts for. That's the gap between coffee alone and both together that we saw a moment ago. A sliver only coffee accounts for. And the biggest part either one could account for on its own. That's the overlap between them.
:::
::::

:::::

We can check the misses just as we did before. Two students had those same six hours and one and a half cups. Both now get a prediction of 63. Their scores were 50 and 65, so their residuals are $-13$ and $+2$.

| Coffee ($X$) | Sleep ($Z$) | Score ($Y$) | $\hat{Y}$ | $Y - \hat{Y}$ | $(Y - \hat{Y})^2$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 9 | 90 | 84 | $6$ | 36 |
| 0.5 | 8 | 60 | 77 | $-17$ | 289 |
| 0.5 | 8 | 85 | 77 | $8$ | 64 |
| 1 | 5 | 65 | 58 | $7$ | 49 |
| 1.5 | 6 | 50 | 63 | $-13$ | 169 |
| 1.5 | 6 | 65 | 63 | $2$ | 4 |
| 2 | 7 | 75 | 68 | $7$ | 49 |

: Predicted values and residuals with both coffee and sleep as predictors. $SS_{residual} = 660$. {#tbl-multiple-residuals}

We're predicting the same seven scores, so the total sum of squares is still 1200. The residual sum of squares is down to 660, leaving $1200 - 660 = 540$ accounted for by the two predictors together. This time there are two slopes, so regression gets two degrees of freedom. Estimating those slopes and the intercept leaves $7 - 3 = 4$ degrees of freedom for the residual.

::: {#tbl-multiple-regression-summary .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Regression | 540 | 2 | 270 | 1.64 |
| Residual | 660 | 4 | 165 | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | 1200 | 6 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

Summary table for the regression with coffee and sleep as predictors.
:::

$$ R^2 = \frac{SS_{regression}}{SS_Y} = \frac{540}{1200} = .45 $$

With more than one predictor we write this proportion as capital $R^2$. Coffee alone accounted for 25% of the variability in our sample. Coffee and sleep together account for 45%. The overall $F$ tests the two slopes together against a model that just predicts the mean. The null hypothesis is that both slopes are zero in the population. In other words, neither coffee nor sleep would help us predict test scores at all. Here $F(2, 4) = 1.64$, $p = .30$. Adding a predictor can improve the fit to the students we already have even if it wouldn't help us predict how new students will score.

       - Add coffee: R^2 = .45 (it can never go down), but MS_reg is now split over 2 df and MS_res over 4,
         so F(2, 4) = 1.64, p = .30.

::: {#quiz-regression-what-sleep-adds}
{{< include quizzes/18-regression-what-sleep-adds.qmd >}}
:::

How much does *coffee* add once we know about sleep? For these seven students, the correlation between sleep and score was about $.67$. So sleep alone accounts for about 44% of the variability. Going from sleep alone to sleep *and* coffee takes us from about 44% to 45%. That's the same story we got from the small partial correlation in Chapter 17, now told in terms of what coffee adds to our predictions. (In Chapter 17 we used all 300 students, and the partial correlation was $-.05$. For these seven students it works out to $-.10$.)

<!-- DRAFT -->
### Testing each predictor

The overall $F$ tells us whether the two predictors together do better than the mean. But we'll usually want to know about each one too. And we've already seen the pieces we need. In the last step of the activity, the 540 split into a part only sleep accounts for, 240, a part only coffee accounts for, 6.67, and a part either one could account for, 293.33. Each predictor's own part is what it adds once the other is already in the equation. So we test it the same way we tested each factor in Chapter 16. Its own sum of squares, with one degree of freedom, goes over the mean square for the residual, which plays the part the within-groups mean square played there.

$$ F_{sleep} = \frac{240}{165} = 1.45 \qquad F_{coffee} = \frac{6.67}{165} = 0.04 $$

Each has 1 and 4 degrees of freedom. Neither comes close to significance: $p = .29$ for sleep and $p = .85$ for coffee.^[Statistical software usually reports a $t$ for each slope rather than an $F$. It's the slope divided by its standard error, and $t^2 = F$, just like before. The standard error is the same formula we used for one predictor, $\sqrt{MS_{residual}/SS}$, but with the sum of squares for that predictor's residuals. For coffee that's $\sqrt{165 / 1.67} = 9.95$, so $t = -2/9.95 = -0.20$. For sleep it's $\sqrt{165 / 6.67} = 4.97$, so $t = 6/4.97 = 1.21$.]

Notice that the shared 293.33 doesn't go to either test. Neither predictor gets credit for it, because either one could account for it without the other. In Chapter 16 that didn't come up. With the same number of scores in every group, the factors aren't related to each other, so there's nothing to share, and the pieces add up neatly. With predictors like coffee and sleep that go together, it's possible for the two of them together to predict significantly better than the mean, while neither one is significant on its own.

<!-- DRAFT -->
### What the slopes mean

Each slope is in the units we measured. With sleep in the equation, the slope for coffee says that for students who got the same amount of sleep, each extra cup goes with a test score 2 points lower. And for students who drank the same amount of coffee, each extra hour of sleep goes with a score 6 points higher.

But notice how much the coffee slope changed, from $-10$ on its own to $-2$ with sleep. A slope in multiple regression always depends on what else is in the equation. Add another predictor that's related to coffee and the coffee slope could change again.^[Because cups and hours are different units, you can't compare the two slopes directly. Software often also reports *standardized* slopes, which are the slopes you'd get if every variable were first converted to $z$-scores. Here they're $-.10$ for coffee and $.60$ for sleep.]

And just as with partial correlations in Chapter 17, holding sleep constant is something we're doing statistically, not experimentally. It tells us what coffee adds to our predictions once we know about sleep. It doesn't tell us whether coffee or sleep causes anything. Other things we didn't measure could still be behind the relationships. That's still a job for random assignment.

## What if the predictor is a group?

Think back to the two spending groups in Chapter 12. Suppose we coded spending on yourself as 0 and spending on someone else as 1, and used that number to predict happiness. What would the least-squares line do? At 0, its best guess would be the mean for the first group. At 1, its best guess would be the mean for the second. Moving one unit along that line takes us from one group mean to the other, so the slope is just the difference between them. Each person's residual is their deviation from their own group mean, exactly the quantity we used for within-groups variability in ANOVA.

So if we tested whether that slope was zero, we'd be asking whether the two group means were equal. That's the question we answered with an independent-samples $t$ test in Chapter 12 and with ANOVA in Chapter 14. With cups of coffee as our predictor, testing the slope brought us back to Chapter 17's test of the correlation. There's a name for the mathematical framework these procedures share. It's called the **general linear model**.

<!-- REVIEW: In the same spirit, r^2 here is also eta^2 from a one-way ANOVA on the two groups (the point-biserial
     r = .28 from Ch 17's footnote gives r^2 = .08). A sentence or the roadmap's closing table
     (t → d, F → eta^2, r → r^2, R^2) would make the effect sizes part of the same family. -->


We started with questions like “Did the two groups differ?” and “Do these two things go together?” Those are still different things we might want to know. But by now you've seen how far we can get with the same few tools you first met with a single mean. Make a prediction, see how far the scores fall from it, and ask how much better we can do with the information we have.
